title: Redwood cost-econ discovery with Crestwood Ventures
summary: Discovery focused on cost/unit economics for Crestwood's LLM workloads. Main asks: predictable unit cost, latency SLOs for real-time features, ability to run on VPC for compliance, and options for committed capacity. Discussed batching, prefix/KV cache, quantization tradeoffs, and a proposed pilot (week-long benchmark) to measure token/unit cost with their prompt mix.
next_steps: Laura to send tailored pricing sheet and committed capacity worksheet
Diego to share benchmark spreadsheet and sample workload runner (small perf harness)
Customer to provide typical prompt set and QPS profile by 2026-03-09
Schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2026-03-16
action_items: Laura: send pricing deck + two committed capacity options (due 2026-03-06)
Diego: upload benchmark spreadsheet and example runbook link (due 2026-03-05)
Ravi: share sample prompts + 95th pct length distribution (due 2026-03-09)

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 40m
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Evan Park (Crestwood CTO), Maya Singh (Eng Manager), Ravi Desai (ML Lead), Anita Cole (Finance)

Summary (auto): cost and unit economics focused discovery with ask for pilot and pricing.

[00:00] Laura Chen: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, uh we wanted to kick off, like, cost-econ chat - mostly around hosted vs dedicated and how batching/caching changes your per token economics.
[00:20] Evan Park: yeah thanks, um quick context, we run an embed+chat feature in our product, about 400k users monthly, spikes up to 250 QPS for interactive chat, average prompt length is 80 tokens, completions ~120 tokens. Budget is roughly $15k-30k/month for inference right now.
[00:45] Maya Singh: and we're storage sensitive - some user data is regulated so VPC or private deployment is a hard ask for a subset of customers.
[01:05] Diego Morales: got it, thanks. just to set expectations, costs change a lot based on three levers: batching (tokens per request batching), KV/prefix cache hit rate (we call it KV cache sometimes transcribed as K-V cash), and quantization/model variant. for hosted we have per-token pricing, for dedicated it's committed capacity with unit economics usually better at scale.
[01:30] Ravi Desai: can you give numbers - like what per 1k tokens we'd be looking at hosted vs dedicated?
[01:45] Laura Chen: yeah, so rough ballpark - hosted API for our curated open models ranges from $0.6 to $1.8 per 1k prompt+completion tokens depending on model size and generation costs; dedicated reserved capacity can push equivalent unit to ~0.25-0.6 per 1k tokens if you utilize batch and caching effectively. caveat: these are ballpark, will send formal sheet.
[02:10] Anita Cole: that delta is big - what drives that?
[02:20] Diego Morales: mostly utilization and batching. with dedicated you control GPU pools so you can run high throughput kernels and continuous batching; with prefix/KV caching if you see repeated prefixes (common in chat) you save a lot of compute. also quantization to int8/4 reduces compute cost but impacts latency and sometimes accuracy.
[02:45] Evan Park: our team cares about latency - interactive chat target is p95 under 300ms. can you hit that with batching? feels like batching increases latency.
[03:05] Diego Morales: right, batching trades latency for throughput. our runtime supports dynamic batching with latency SLOs - you can set a max latency target (e.g., 200-300ms) and we will only batch up to the point that meets that SLO. plus we have prefix cache which doesn't add batching delay for cache hits. so if you get a high cache hit rate, you get both low latency and lower cost.
[03:35] Maya Singh: what's realistic cache hit rate - 30, 50%?
[03:40] Diego Morales: depends on patterns. chat applications with repeated system prompts or templates can see 40-70% prefix hit; question/answer patterns less so. we'll want sample prompts to estimate.
[03:55] Evan Park: okay, sample prompts we'll share. what's the pilot look like?
[04:05] Laura Chen: typical pilot is 1 week benchmark: you provide sample prompt set + QPS profile; we run hosted and a dedicated sim with similar VM sizes to measure p50/p95 latency and cost per 1k tokens using your mix. Diego: add details?
[04:20] Diego Morales: yes, we'll run three modes: hosted (our standard), dedicated with default batching, dedicated with aggressive batching + cache priming. we'll measure throughput, latency, and cost per 1k tokens. Deliverable: benchmark spreadsheet + config and run logs.
[04:40] Ravi Desai: how do you price dedicated - is it flat reserved GPU monthly fee or tokens on top?
[04:50] Laura Chen: dedicated is committed capacity - you pay for reserved pool (monthly) and then usage sits inside that pool; we typically model effective price per 1k tokens based on expected utilization. if you go above reserved capacity we have burst rates.
[05:05] Anita Cole: what's the commitment length? and are there discounts for annual?
[05:10] Laura Chen: we do 6-12 month commits, with better pricing and capacity guarantees for longer terms. we'll outline two options in the sheet: a smaller reserved pool + burst vs larger pool with lower unit rate.
[05:25] Evan Park: security - for our regulated clients we need customer-managed KMS and audit logs. can dedicated handle that?
[05:35] Diego Morales: yes, our Private deployment supports customer KMS/HSM and full audit logs. Dedicated (hosted but reserved) has options for KMS integrations and VPC peering depending on the tier. we'll map exact security features for the planned pilot.
[05:55] Maya Singh: do you support on-prem? we've seen that term thrown around.
[06:00] Laura Chen: we do a private on-prem option - more complex procurement and infra work, usually for enterprises. might be overkill initially.
[06:10] Evan Park: any gotchas around tokenization differences - we use UTF-8 multi-lang prompts?
[06:18] Diego Morales: tokenization can affect token counts up to ~10-15% depending on language - we'll tokenize your samples to get accurate cost projections.
[06:30] Maya Singh: pricing sensitivity: Anita, finance, do you have hard limits?
[06:34] Anita Cole: we want to keep ops spend for inference under $25k month for pilots. long term we could go up depending on ROI.
[06:45] Laura Chen: that's helpful. using that we can size a pilot that shows where you'd land.
[06:55] Evan Park: any competitors we should be benchmarking against? we're talking to OpenAI + Anthropic for hosted API, and a couple vendors doing infra.
[07:05] Laura Chen: fair. we'll include OpenAI/Anthropic baseline pricing in the comparison and call out where dedicated capacity changes the picture.
[07:15] Diego Morales: technical note - for throughput, what GPU type do you foresee? current roughs assume A10G/A100 equivalence; if you have lower-end GPUs that affects unit price.
[07:30] Ravi Desai: our infra team prefers A10G-ish for cost reasons, not full A100.
[07:35] Diego Morales: that's fine, we'll model both.
[07:45] Maya Singh: can you explain the math - how batching and cache translate to per-1k token cost? maybe a simple example.
[07:55] Laura Chen: sure - imagine a baseline where a model costs $X per GPU-hour. If you can batch requests so that each GPU step processes more tokens, your tokens per GPU-hour increases, lowering cost/token. caching avoids recomputation for prefix tokens entirely, so cache-hit tokens are effectively near-zero compute cost (still storage/serving cost). so a 50% cache hit rate can cut effective compute cost by ~30-40% depending on batch size and sequence lengths. we'll show worked examples in the worksheet.
[08:35] Evan Park: ok so how often do you see customer perf diverge from modeled numbers?
[08:40] Diego Morales: sometimes when prompt distributions are heavy-tail or there are many multimodal prompts; that's why we insist on real sample prompts for the pilot.
[08:50] Laura Chen: also quantization - int8 gets you lower cost but you may need evals for quality regressions. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles per workload.
[09:05] Ravi Desai: can you do A/B where some traffic uses quantized model and some uses full fp16 with fallback on quality issues?
[09:12] Diego Morales: yes, rollouts and automatic fallback are supported. you can do canary + fallback if a quality metric crosses threshold.
[09:25] Maya Singh: on procurement, Anita, timeline?
[09:28] Anita Cole: if pilot looks good, procurement after quarter-end; need SOC2 docs and standard contract review.
[09:35] Laura Chen: we'll attach SOC2 and security pack with the follow-up.
[09:40] Evan Park: okay logistics - what do you need from us to start the pilot?
[09:45] Laura Chen: three things: sample prompt set + typical QPS profile, target latency SLOs and budget constraint, and a contact for infra to coordinate VPC/credentials.
[10:00] Evan Park: we'll get that by Monday.
[10:05] Diego Morales: quick question on evaluation metrics - we'll capture cost per 1k tokens, p50/p95 latency, and SU (service utilization) of reserved pool.
[10:20] Ravi Desai: thanks. and can you include an example showing the impact of increasing batch window from 10ms to 50ms on p95?
[10:28] Diego Morales: yes, we'll include param sweeps in the spreadsheet.
[10:35] Anita Cole: about billing - is there visibility into token-level spend in console?
[10:40] Laura Chen: yes, Redwood Console shows token-level cost, per-route, per-model breakdown and can export CSV.
[10:48] Evan Park: any third-party surprises like egress or networking costs?
[10:53] Diego Morales: for hosted, egress only if you move data out of region; for private/on-prem you control networking. we'll call out potential cloud egress.
[11:05] Maya Singh: sounds good. any outstanding technical risks?
[11:10] Diego Morales: main risk is tokenization/length mismatch and unseen distribution tails. pilot mitigates that.
[11:20] Laura Chen: recap - we'll send pricing deck + committed options, Diego shares benchmark spreadsheet and run plan, Crestwood shares prompts + QPS, and we'll plan a 1-week pilot starting week of 2026-03-16.
[11:40] Evan Park: good, thanks everyone.
[11:42] Laura Chen: thanks, we'll follow up with calendar invite and artifacts.

Notes: occasional transcription errors present (e.g., K-V cash), speaker overlap minimal. Shared artifacts mentioned: pricing deck link (to be sent), benchmark spreadsheet (to be uploaded).
